A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question b, other: The clue 'Think about what lies between the particles' points straight at the only option about the gaps between particles, so a student could pick the right answer without knowing the idea.

rejected.title: The particle theory of matter
card: All matter is made of tiny particles. Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass.
The particles are always moving. They never stop, even in a solid that looks still.
The particles attract each other. This pull holds them together.
There is space between the particles. The particles are the matter, and the gaps between them are empty.
rejected.remember: Matter is made of tiny moving particles that attract each other and have space between them.

a.q: A block of wood looks completely still. What does the particle theory say about its particles?
opts: They are always moving, though the block looks still
They are not moving, because the block is still
They are moving only when the block is heated
They are moving only when the block is touched
a.why: The theory says particles are always moving, so the particles in the block move even though it looks still. Saying they move only when heated is tempting, but the card says the movement never stops.
a.clue: Look at what the card says about how long particles move.

b.q: Mei says the water in a glass is one continuous piece with no gaps at all. Which idea from the particle theory shows she is wrong?
opts: There is space between the particles of water
The particles of water have stopped moving
Water is not made of particles at all
The particles of water do not attract each other
b.why: The theory says there is space between the particles, so water is not one continuous piece with no gaps. The idea that the particles do not attract is wrong, because the theory says they pull on each other.
b.clue: Think about what lies between the particles.

flags: Question b, other: The clue 'Think about what lies between the particles' points straight at the only option about the gaps between particles, so a student could pick the right answer without knowing the idea.

problems.detail: Mei calls water 'solid all the way through'. Water is a liquid, and solids, liquids and gases are taught in the next point, so the everyday sense of 'solid' (meaning 'no gaps') could confuse students. Something like 'made of one continuous piece with no gaps' would be clearer.

check.summary: The facts and answers are correct. One minor wording issue: question b describes water as 'solid', which could confuse students who are about to learn states of matter.

opts: They keep moving, even though the spoon looks still

They start moving only when the spoon is heated up
They start moving only when someone picks up the spoon

b.q: Sam says a drop of water is one smooth piece, with nothing at all between its parts. Which idea from the particle theory shows he is wrong?
opts: There is space between the particles of water
The particles of water have stopped moving
Water is not made of particles at all
The particles of water do not attract each other
b.why: The theory says there is space between the particles, so water is not one smooth piece with nothing between its parts. The idea that the particles do not attract is wrong, because the theory says they pull on each other.
b.clue: Sam's claim is about how the water is built, not how it moves.
